title: Phage proteases activate CBASS antiphage immunity.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: The Science article itself is closed (Europe PMC: not open access, no full text). I found and read the matching bioRxiv preprint full text in PMC (PMC12991175), downloaded its complete 4.3 MB supplementary archive, and extracted the text of all 5 supplementary pages. The entire machine-readable content is Table S1: 12 rows (12 CD-NTase enzymes, an enzyme family that makes bacterial immune signalling molecules), with columns clade, cluster number, NCBI protein accession, alternative name, species, Whiteley-et-al enzyme number, and the protein concentration used in Figure 4. All other data are gel, thin-layer-chromatography and plaque-assay images. I also searched the full text for a data availability statement, PDB (Protein Data Bank) depositions, Zenodo, Dryad and GitHub: none are present. The structure predictions were made on the public AlphaFold3 web server and were not deposited.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The in-vitro and in-vivo activation results themselves (which of the 12 enzymes are activated by proteinase K, the efficiency-of-plaquing values for phages Bas48-59, the western-blot cleavage sizes) are read off figure panels and their legends; none of these numbers exist as a table I could open. I did not fetch the Science-version supplementary materials, since the publisher site is out of scope and the preprint supplement is the same set of figures plus Table S1.

a1_downloadable.note: Supplement downloads freely from Europe PMC for the preprint version (4.3 MB zip: four figure images plus one 5-page PDF). No login needed. But there is no data repository deposit of any kind.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. The outcome of interest - whether a given CD-NTase enzyme is switched on by protease cleavage, and how strongly - appears only as bands on thin-layer-chromatography plates in Figure 4B. Table S1 has no activation column at all; its only numeric column is the protein concentration used in the assay. The label would have to be constructed by eye from gel images.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are retrievable: Table S1 gives NCBI protein accessions for all 12 enzymes, so sequences are 12 lookups away, not thousands. Sequences themselves are not in the file.

a4_units_stated.note: The one numeric column has explicit units (50 nM or 5 micromolar). Figure axes state units too, but figures are images.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL, decisively. Twelve enzymes in Table S1 (four representative sequences from each of three clades, A, D and G), counted by me in the file. The checklist floor is ~400 rows even for pure classification. A dozen phages (Bas48-59) are screened in Figure S3B, which is the same order of magnitude.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially small; the whole supplement is four images and one PDF.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Table S1's 12 rows match the paper's description of four cluster representatives per clade across clades A, D and G.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels come from real biochemistry (thin-layer chromatography of nucleotide synthesis, plaque assays, western blots), not from another model's output. Provenance is clean; there is just almost none of it. Note the structural figures use AlphaFold3 predictions, so any structure-derived feature would be model output.

existing_models.name: DefensePredictor (2025) - classifies bacterial proteins as immune-defence proteins from protein language model embeddings
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported on 69 diverse E. coli strains; predicted hundreds of candidate systems with 42 experimentally validated. Exact split and metric not read by me - I only retrieved the abstract.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not read; I did not retrieve the discussion.

existing_models.name: Protein and genomic language models for antiphage defence (bioRxiv 2025) - fine-tuned ESM-2 plus an ALBERT-architecture genomic language model
existing_models.score_and_split: Scanned over 30,000 bacterial genomes and nominated more than 45,000 uncharacterised protein families as candidate defence components; six systems experimentally validated. Metrics not retrieved.

existing_models.name: ProsperousPlus / Procleave / DeepCleave - protease-specific cleavage-site predictors (relevant to the cleavage half of the mechanism, trained on human caspases and metalloproteases, not phage prohead proteases)
existing_models.score_and_split: Published average area-under-the-curve of 0.966 (ProsperousPlus), 0.950 (Procleave) and 0.923 (DeepCleave) across the proteases they cover; split details not retrieved.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (a protein language model that turns an amino-acid sequence into a numeric vector; small checkpoints run on a laptop CPU)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU would be ample for 12 sequences, which is exactly the problem - 12 examples cannot train or honestly evaluate any head.
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT-licensed; the paper's own supplement is CC-BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial).

integration.partner_dataset: Supplementary Table 2 of Whiteley et al., Nature 2019 - the ~6,000-member catalogue of CD-NTase enzymes that this paper drew its 12 representatives from; joinable by NCBI protein accession and by the 'Whiteley CD-NTase number' column that Table S1 already carries.
integration.join_key: NCBI protein accession (e.g. WP_000064266.1) plus the Whiteley CD-NTase number
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Which of the thousands of known CD-NTase enzymes carry a protease-cleavable activation loop, and therefore which bacteria can sense a phage by its packaging protease? - but the 12 measured answers in this paper are far too few to train or test that predictor, so the join supplies features with no labels.

controls.positive_control: EcCdnG itself, the enzyme characterised in depth here, would have to be recovered as protease-activated by any working model.
controls.negative_control: The catalytically dead EcCdnG D82/84A mutant, which Figure S2C shows is not activated by any protease.
controls.external_validation: The 2024 Cell Host & Microbe large-scale type I CBASS screen (which independently flagged the phage prohead protease as the key determinant of immune activation and evasion) is a genuinely independent source, but I did not open its data to check whether it is tabulated.

honest_claim_h3: With 12 enzymes, the only honest claim available is descriptive - 'these particular 12 CD-NTases behave this way' - not a predictive one; no model trained here could claim to generalise to unseen enzymes.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a bacterial immune enzyme's sequence to predict whether a virus's packaging protease can switch it on.
plain_idea.train_on: The amino-acid sequence of each CD-NTase enzyme (a bacterial enzyme that makes an immune alarm signal), plus the position of its surface-exposed activation loop. Verified count of labelled examples: 12.
plain_idea.predict: Yes/no, or how strongly, the enzyme starts making its nucleotide alarm signal after a protease cuts it. The true answer comes from thin-layer chromatography of radiolabelled nucleotide products after treating the purified enzyme with proteinase K - read off gel images in Figure 4B.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Phage-therapy and bacterial-immunity groups would want to know, for any sequenced bacterium, whether its CBASS system can be triggered by a phage's own packaging enzyme - which would predict which phages that bacterium can resist. Even a failed model would map how far activation-loop presence can be read from sequence alone.

more_or_better_data.why: This paper contributes 12 measured enzymes. DefensePredictor and the ESM-2/genomic-language-model work operate over tens of thousands of genomes, so our data is four orders of magnitude smaller than theirs.

confidence_score.why: No replicate measurements are tabulated - figure panels say 'representative' gel - so per-prediction uncertainty cannot be estimated from these files.

models_beatable.why: Not applicable in any useful sense: with 12 labelled examples there is no training or test set, so no comparison against DefensePredictor (2025, protein language model embeddings) could be made.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails on the first condition - there is no baseline to run on this task, and no evaluation split is possible with 12 rows.

ml_idea: Considered: predict from a CD-NTase amino-acid sequence (via frozen ESM-2 embeddings) whether the enzyme has a protease-cleavable activation loop and is switched on by phage prohead protease activity, then scan the ~6,000 CD-NTases in the Whiteley et al. 2019 catalogue for sensors of phage proteases. Dead on arrival here: the paper supplies 12 labelled enzymes and the labels exist only as bands in gel images.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: 12 sequences through a small ESM-2 checkpoint on a laptop CPU is minutes. Cross-validation time is null because 12 examples do not support a meaningful cross-validation run.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in Table S1 - the one and only machine-readable table in the whole supplement. I did it: 12. That kills it in five minutes.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A5 (enough rows) and A2 (label is a column). The entire tabular output of this paper is a 12-row supplementary table of CD-NTase enzyme identifiers, and the thing we would predict - whether protease cleavage switches the enzyme on - exists only as bands on thin-layer-chromatography and gel images, not as a column anywhere. There is no repository deposit, no PDB structure (the structural figures are undeposited AlphaFold3 web-server predictions), and no sequencing data. It is an excellent, important piece of mechanistic biochemistry whose data footprint is images; the interesting predictive question (which of ~6,000 known CD-NTases carry a cleavable activation loop) would need a screen two or three orders of magnitude larger than this paper's 12 enzymes.
